raw_case_text: A 50-year-old male, smoker (50 p/y), with a history of alcoholism, severe COPD, bilateral pneumothorax, and tuberculosis due to mycobacterium avium infection, was admitted in our department eight months after antituberculosis treatment initialization due to one-month period of high fever, up to 39.6 C, loss of weight, almost 5 kgr, and productive cough with purulent sputum (Figures 1 and 2). Despite adequate treatment with antibiotics, in outpatient setting, he remained with no clinical improvement. Routine laboratory tests on admission revealed increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR = 134 mm/hr) and C-reactive protein (CRP = 112 mg/dL). A chest X-ray demonstrated cavitations, consolidation, and fibrosis at both upper lobes. Serologic tests for hepatitis A, B, C, D, and human immunodeficiency virus did not reveal any abnormality. Broad spectrum antibiotics were initialized during his hospitalization without any improvement. Finally in three different sputum samples Aspergillus flavius was isolated and, a CT scan demonstrated cavitary lesions with shadows, probably due to fungus contamination inside them, especially in the upper left lobe (Figures 3 and 4). These facts established a diagnosis of chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis. Treatment with amphotericin B provided an initial clinical improvement but eleven days after a first episode of mild hemoptysis occurred and was controlled with conservative measures. Eighteen days after treatment initialization a second episode of hemoptysis occurred and, although he was intubated immediately, his cardiorespiratory system collapsed and he died.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old male presenting with high fever, weight loss, and productive purulent cough for one month.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented 8 months into antituberculosis treatment with a 1-month history of high fever up to 39.6 °C, weight loss of approximately 5 kg, and a productive cough with purulent sputum. Outpatient oral antibiotic therapy produced no clinical improvement. Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics initiated upon admission were also ineffective. Eleven days following initiation of antifungal therapy, he suffered an initial mild episode of hemoptysis controlled with conservative measures; 18 days after antifungal initiation, he developed a second catastrophic episode of hemoptysis leading to cardiorespiratory arrest.
subjective.past_medical_history: 50 pack-year cigarette smoking history, chronic alcoholism, severe COPD, history of bilateral pneumothorax, and pulmonary mycobacterial infection (Mycobacterium avium) treated with antituberculosis medications for 8 months.
subjective.review_of_systems: High-grade fever up to 39.6 °C, progressive weight loss (5 kg), purulent productive cough, recurrent hemoptysis.

objective.physical_examination: Patient was acutely ill and febrile with temperatures reaching 39.6 °C.
objective.routine_investigations: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 134 mm/hr; C-reactive protein (CRP) was 112 mg/dL. Serologic tests for hepatitis A, B, C, D, and HIV were negative. Chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral upper lobe cavitations, consolidations, and fibrotic changes.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracic CT scan demonstrated large upper lobe cavitary lesions containing intracavitary dependent densities/masses consistent with fungal balls, particularly in the left upper lobe.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis (CCPA) with Aspergillus flavus colonization and intracavitary fungal ball formation in pre-existing mycobacterial cavities, complicated by fatal massive hemoptysis.
Diagnostic confirmation: Isolation of Aspergillus flavus from three independent sputum cultures, supported by CT visualization of intracavitary shadows in chronic bilateral upper lobe cavities.
Management and outcome: Unresponsive to outpatient and inpatient broad-spectrum antibacterial agents. Intravenous amphotericin B was initiated, yielding initial clinical stabilization. However, an initial episode of mild hemoptysis occurred on day 11, followed on day 18 by sudden massive pulmonary hemorrhage; despite immediate endotracheal intubation, cardiorespiratory collapse ensued and the patient died.
